entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
David, known posthumously as Saint David (Dewi Sant in Welsh), emerged as a pivotal figure in 6th-century Wales, serving as Bishop of Mynyw (modern St Davids) and profoundly shaping the trajectory of early Welsh Christianity. His life, though shrouded in the mists of early medieval hagiography, solidified the monastic tradition and ecclesiastical structure across what would become Wales, establishing him as the nation's enduring patron saint. Operating within the dynamic post-Roman British landscape, David's influence extended beyond spiritual leadership, contributing to the distinct cultural and religious identity of the Welsh people.

Central to David's historical footprint was his fervent advocacy for ascetic monasticism, reportedly founding numerous monasteries throughout Wales, Brittany, and even Ireland. His most significant foundation was at Mynyw, which became a prominent spiritual center. Accounts, most notably Rhygyfarch's 11th-century *Vita Sancti Davidis*, describe David's rigorous practices, including a vegetarian diet, manual labor, and prolonged prayer, inspiring a generation of followers. He is also traditionally credited with presiding over the Synod of Brefi (c. 545 CE), which condemned Pelagianism and affirmed orthodox Christian doctrine in Wales, solidifying the nascent Welsh church's theological stance amidst broader European religious currents.
